items.q: I left on my 18th birthday and I went to Chicago to join King Oliver's band.

ctx.x: No, it's gone now. It was so old and when she died they had so many children to be divided that they couldn't wait to get a decent price for it, so they had it up for auction. So they practically got nothing for it, and that's the way it went, a very cheap modest price. It was practically rotten.
And that's when well, I had I left on my 18th birthday and I went to Chicago to join King Oliver's band.

Oh.

What playing had you done in New Orleans?

items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, 1969-07-25
items.q: And I was working with King Oliver at the time.

ctx.x: Hi Bill, this is Floyd Levin in Los Angeles. This is the 25th of July 1969 and shortly I expect Barney Begard over, at which time I will supply the questions and hopefully he'll come up with some of the answers to help you on your quest for information about Jelly Roll Morton. Okay, we've just played the Victor Trio session, Barney. I assume that you have some memories about that session. Yeah, I was really surprised. I thought I played more than I do now. That's going back, what, 40 years? Yes, it is. Could you…
. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. That's okay. You can cut that off. One. Two. You see, if you count and then pick back the notes up, it screws you up. Yeah. ¶ Thank you.

items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, Early 1970s
items.q: King Alva got a place at the, a job at the plantation. Mm-hm. And they did everything in their power to keep, keeping from bringing a band in there, but he made a triumph, and the people just loved him. And we stayed there for quite some time.

ctx.x: What was the first recording made that you recall? Your first recording, who was it made with?

It was made with, uh, made in Chicago, with a guy named, uh, My Knee Jones, he was a peg-legged pianist. Mm-hm. And, uh, well, in fact, when I went to Chicago, and I was supposed to go to work with King Alva, it was near the end, and the place where we were going to work, we were supposed to start on the Christmas Eve, and it burned down. Mm-hm. So we were sort of stranded. And this, uh, fellow, My Knee Jones, he was from New Orleans, and he was a writer, composer. And he had little gigs, and he found out that we…
What was it that inspired you to go into music, Marnie Begard?
